text: Which of these countries is NOT a member of the G7 group of major industrialised economies?
solution: The G7 is the United States, Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy and Canada. China, despite the size of its economy, is not a member; it belongs to the wider G20.

text: Which ancient Greek writer is known as the "father of history"?
solution: Herodotus, in the 5th century BC, wrote the Histories, an inquiry into the Persian Wars that gave the subject its name; Cicero called him the father of history. Thucydides wrote on the Peloponnesian War, Homer composed epic poems, Plutarch wrote biographies under the Romans, and Pericles was an Athenian statesman.

text:
Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) gives medical care to people affected by conflict, epidemics and disasters, guided by medical ethics, impartiality, independence and neutrality.
Which one of the following would be INCONSISTENT with these principles?
options: Treating patients regardless of their race, religion or politics
Treating those in the greatest medical need first
Treating patients from the side of a conflict that the organisation supports before others
Speaking out publicly about the suffering its staff witness
Refusing funding that would limit its independence
solution: Impartiality and neutrality mean care is given according to need alone, without taking sides, so favouring one side of a conflict breaks both. Treating everyone regardless of background and treating the most urgent cases first follow from impartiality; bearing witness and protecting independence are also part of the organisation's principles.

text:
A bag holds 4 blue counters, 2 white counters and 1 black counter. Without looking, I take out a blue counter and then the black counter, and I do not put them back.
Which one of the following statements must be true?
options: The next counter could be black.
The next counter will definitely be blue.
The next two counters cannot both be white.
At least one of the next three counters must be blue.
At least one of the next three counters must be white.
solution: The bag now holds 3 blue and 2 white. Any three counters can include at most the 2 whites, so at least one must be blue. The black has gone, the next one could be white, both whites could come next, and three blues in a row is possible, so no white is guaranteed.

text:
I want to buy two different books for three children, Rosa, Sam and Tilly, to share. Each child must like at least one of the two books, I do not want hardbacks, and I want to spend as little as possible.

| book | hardback? | liked by Rosa? | liked by Sam? | liked by Tilly? | price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| atlas | yes | yes | yes | no | €15 |
| comic | no | yes | no | no | €6 |
| novel | no | no | yes | yes | €10 |
| puzzle book | no | no | no | yes | €5 |
| cookbook | no | yes | yes | no | €9 |

How much will I pay?
solution: Leave out the hardback atlas. Pairs that please all three: comic + novel (€16), cookbook + novel (€19) and cookbook + puzzle book (€14). Comic + puzzle book (€11) is cheaper but leaves Sam with nothing he likes. The cheapest suitable pair costs €14.

text: In a city of ancient Greece, what was the agora?
options: the main public square, used as a market and a meeting place
the wall that defended the city
a council of elders that advised the king
solution: The agora was the open heart of a Greek city: a market, a place for public business and debate, and the setting for much of civic life. Temples stood on sacred sites such as the acropolis, plays were performed in the theatre, and a council of elders was a body of people, not a place.

text: Which set of statements about Galileo Galilei is correct?
options: he was born in Florence, was an astronomer, died before 1600
he was born in Pisa, used a telescope to observe the moons of Jupiter, was tried by the Inquisition
he was born in Rome, was a painter, died in 1520
he was born in Pisa, discovered the circulation of the blood, died in Padua
he was born in Venice, wrote poetry, was a monk
solution: Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564, discovered Jupiter's four largest moons with his telescope in 1610, and was tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 for supporting the idea that the Earth moves round the Sun; he died in 1642. The circulation of the blood was described by William Harvey, who had studied at Padua.

text: Which of the following is NOT true of the Renaissance?
options: It began in Italy in the 14th and 15th centuries.
It revived interest in the art and learning of ancient Greece and Rome.
It was driven by the Church rejecting classical learning.
Artists such as Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo worked during it.
The printing press helped to spread its ideas.
solution: The Renaissance revived classical learning rather than rejecting it, and popes and churchmen were among its greatest patrons. It began in Italian cities such as Florence, produced artists like Leonardo and Michelangelo, and spread across Europe with the help of printing from the mid-15th century.

text:
Two lighthouses can be seen from a beach. One flashes every 12 seconds and the other every 18 seconds. They have just flashed at the same moment.
How long will it be before they next flash together?
solution: They flash together again after the lowest common multiple of 12 and 18. Multiples of 18 are 18, 36, 54...; the first that is also a multiple of 12 is 36, so 36 seconds. 216 is the product of 12 and 18, a common multiple but not the lowest.

text:
Staff at a warehouse are paid €12 an hour on weekdays, one and a half times that rate on Saturdays and twice that rate on Sundays. Last week they worked these hours:

| | weekdays | Saturday | Sunday |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ana | 30 | 6 | 4 |
| Ben | 34 | 4 | 3 |
| Cara | 24 | 8 | 5 |
| Dev | 36 | 2 | 2 |
| Eli | 28 | 6 | 6 |

Who earned the most?
solution: Count each person's hours at the weekday rate: Ana 30 + 9 + 8 = 47, Ben 34 + 6 + 6 = 46, Cara 24 + 12 + 10 = 46, Dev 36 + 3 + 4 = 43, Eli 28 + 9 + 12 = 49. Eli earned most (49 x €12 = €588), even though Dev worked the most hours.

text:
A teacher sets her six-digit locker code like this: first the two digits of her birth month, reversed (so March, 03, becomes 30); then the number of pupils in her class, which is always between 20 and 30; then the two digits of her day of birth, reversed (so the 7th, 07, becomes 70).
Which one of the following could NOT be her code?
solution: The first pair must be a month reversed: 10, 20, ... 90 for January to September, or 01, 11, 21 for October to December. 31 reversed is 13, which is not a month, so 312570 is impossible. The others work: July, 28, the 31st; November, 22, the 15th; October, 23, the 29th; September, 25, the 7th.

text:
Lockers line both walls of a corridor. They are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... along one wall, and the numbering carries on back down the opposite wall, so the last locker faces locker 1. Each locker faces exactly one other. Locker 13 faces locker 40.
How many lockers are there?
solution: With n lockers, locker k faces locker n + 1 - k (1 faces n, 2 faces n - 1, and so on). So 13 + 40 = n + 1, giving n = 52. Facing numbers always add up to one more than the number of lockers.

text:
A flight attendant works two return trips between Rome and Athens in one day, starting from Rome. After each landing she leaves again on the first departure. The timetable gives local times; Athens is one hour ahead of Rome.

| Rome depart | Athens arrive | Athens depart | Rome arrive |
|---|---|---|---|
| 07:00 | 10:00 | 10:45 | 11:45 |
| 10:30 | 13:30 | 14:15 | 15:15 |
| 13:30 | 16:30 | 17:15 | 18:15 |
| 16:45 | 19:45 | 20:30 | 21:30 |

From her first take-off to her final landing, how long is she on duty?
solution: 07:00 from Rome, back on the 10:45 from Athens at 11:45. The next flight out is 13:30, back on the 17:15 at 18:15. Both take-off and landing are Rome times, so the day lasts from 07:00 to 18:15: 11 hours 15 minutes. The time difference matters only for comparing Athens times with Rome times.

text:
Three shops have offers on the same brand of washing-up liquid:
1 Buy two bottles and get a third free.
2 The normal price of a bottle is cut by one-third.
3 A bottle at the normal price contains 50% extra liquid.
Which offers give the same price per millilitre?
solution: Let a normal bottle cost 1 for 1 unit of liquid. Offer 1: 3 units for 2, so 2/3 per unit. Offer 2: 1 unit for 2/3. Offer 3: 1.5 units for 1, so 1/1.5 = 2/3 per unit. All three give the same price per millilitre.

text:
About 8% of men are colour-blind. The world is designed around people with full colour vision, from traffic lights to maps and charts. So colour-blind people should be classed as having a disability and be given special support.
Which one of the following, if true, weakens this argument?
options: Colour-blind people are not allowed to become airline pilots.
Many maps use colour alone to show information.
Some colour-blind children are wrongly told they are careless.
Colour-blind people reach senior positions in almost every profession as often as anyone else.
solution: The argument assumes that a world designed for the majority puts colour-blind people at a real disadvantage. If they succeed in their careers as often as everyone else, that disadvantage looks small. Being barred from flying, colour-only maps and being misjudged at school all support the argument; inheritance is irrelevant.

text:
In football penalty kicks, goalkeepers dive to one side about 94% of the time. Studies of hundreds of penalties show that about a third of shots go to the middle of the goal, and that a keeper who stays in the centre saves those shots far more often than one who dives. Researchers suggest keepers dive because letting in a goal while standing still would feel worse.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
options: Goalkeepers might save more penalties if they stayed in the centre more often.
A goalkeeper who stays in the centre will always save the penalty.
Penalty takers should always shoot at the middle of the goal.
Goalkeepers cannot control which way they dive.
Goalkeepers can be trained to react faster.
solution: A third of shots go to the middle, and staying in the centre saves those far more often, yet keepers rarely stay, so staying more often could save more penalties. The passage does not say staying always works, does not advise takers, says keepers choose to dive for emotional reasons, and says nothing about reaction training.

text:
A car park charges €3.00 on entry, then €1.20 per hour for the first 5 hours and €0.90 per hour after that. When I left, I paid with a €15 note and received €1.50 change.
How long was the car parked?
solution: I paid €13.50. Taking off the €3.00 entry charge leaves €10.50 for time. The first 5 hours cost €6.00, leaving €4.50 at €0.90 an hour: 5 more hours. Total 10 hours. Forgetting the change gives 11.7 hours.

text:
The table shows a country's water use by sector, in millions of cubic metres.

| sector | 2000 | 2010 | 2020 |
|---|---|---|---|
| agriculture | 420 | 455 | 470 |
| industry | 180 | 170 | 160 |
| households | 150 | 175 | 215 |
| energy | 90 | 120 | 135 |
| other | 20 | 25 | 22 |
| total | 860 | 945 | 1002 |

Which sector contributed most to the rise in total water use between 2000 and 2020?
solution: Total use rose by 142. Changes: agriculture +50, industry -20, households +65, energy +45, other +2. Households contributed most, although agriculture uses by far the most water overall.

text:
If more children walked to school, there would be less traffic outside schools at the start and end of the day, and so cleaner air in the streets around them. Children would get more exercise, which is linked to better concentration in class. They would also learn to handle roads safely while still young, and parents would save time no longer spent driving.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
options: Parents who drive their children to school are lazy.
Cars should be banned from streets near schools.
Walking to school would improve children's health more than any other change.
There would be many benefits if more children walked to school.
Traffic outside schools causes most childhood asthma.
solution: The passage lists one benefit after another (less traffic, cleaner air, exercise, road sense, time saved), so the supported conclusion is that walking would bring many benefits. It does not criticise parents, call for a ban, compare walking with other changes, or say what causes most asthma.

text:
My cousin Ada was born in the year before me, on 1 August; my cousin Ben was born in the year after me, on 25 June. My own birthday is 10 July.
For how many days of the year do I share an age with Ada or with Ben?
solution: Ada is usually a year older, except from my birthday (10 July) until hers (1 August), when we are the same age: 10 to 31 July, 22 days. Ben is usually a year younger, except from his birthday (25 June) until mine: 25 June to 9 July, 15 days. In total 22 + 15 = 37 days.

text:
The table shows the number of members of a sports centre, by age group, who take part in each activity.

| activity | under 30 | 30 to 50 | over 50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| swimming | 30 | 45 | 75 |
| yoga | 20 | 30 | 50 |
| tennis | 25 | 40 | 60 |
| cycling | 40 | 45 | 65 |
| chess | 10 | 20 | 70 |
| running | 50 | 30 | 20 |

In which activity are the proportions of the three age groups closest to those for swimming?
solution: Swimming's groups are 30 : 45 : 75 = 2 : 3 : 5, that is 20%, 30% and 50%. Yoga's 20 : 30 : 50 is exactly 2 : 3 : 5. Tennis is close (20%, 32%, 48%) but not exact; cycling, chess and running are further away. Comparing numbers rather than proportions would point to tennis or cycling.

text:
Pens cost 20c, pencils 30c and rubbers 50c. Omar spends exactly €1.20 on some of them.
Which of these statements are correct?
1 He cannot have exactly 2 rubbers.
2 He must have at least one pencil.
3 He has between 3 and 6 items.
4 If he has all three kinds of item, he has more pens than rubbers.
solution: List every way to make 120c: 4 pencils; 1 pen and 2 rubbers; 2 pens, 1 pencil and 1 rubber; 3 pens and 2 pencils; 6 pens. So 2 rubbers is possible (1 wrong), and 6 pens use no pencil (2 wrong). The item counts are 4, 3, 4, 5 and 6, all between 3 and 6 (3 right). The only mix of all three has 2 pens and 1 rubber (4 right).

text:
Surveys show that fewer people now follow official healthy-eating guidelines, many saying the advice changes too often to be trusted. Yet the population is living longer and suffering less heart disease. This suggests that people know better than nutrition experts what is good for them.
Which one of the following, if true, weakens this argument?
options: Nutrition experts now give advice on a wider range of foods.
People can easily find nutrition advice online.
The improvements in health are concentrated in exactly the areas the guidelines target, such as lower salt intake.
People believe they know better than nutrition experts.
Nutrition experts prefer giving advice to prescribing medicines.
solution: If health has improved precisely where the guidelines aimed, such as less salt and so less heart disease, the guidelines are working, perhaps through food makers or the people who do follow them, rather than people outsmarting the experts. People's beliefs about themselves are not evidence, and the other options do not touch the link between the advice and the improvement.

text:
In 2010 a mother was exactly three times as old as her daughter. In 2025 she will be exactly twice as old as her daughter.
What is the difference between their ages?
solution: If the daughter was d in 2010, the mother was 3d. Fifteen years later: 3d + 15 = 2(d + 15), so d = 15. The mother was 45, and the difference is 45 - 15 = 30 years, the same at every age. In 2025 they will be 60 and 30.

text:
My purse holds five 1c coins, four 2c coins, three 5c coins, two 10c coins, one 20c coin and two 50c coins. A newspaper costs exactly 43c, and I want to pay with the greatest possible number of coins.
How many coins is that?
solution: Use every 1c and 2c coin: 9 coins making 13c. The other 30c must come from the 5c, 10c and 20c coins, and 5 + 5 + 10 + 10 uses 4 of them. No choice uses more: all three 5c coins would leave 15c, which the 10c and 20c coins cannot make. So the most is 9 + 4 = 13 coins.

text:
A choir posts a newsletter (80 g) to all 400 of its members. Its 30 soloists also receive a music score (60 g), and 50 other members, none of them soloists, also receive a survey (40 g). Each envelope weighs 10 g.
Postage: up to 100 g, 50c; up to 150 g, 70c; up to 200 g, 90c.
What is the least the mailing can cost?
solution: A newsletter alone weighs 90 g with its envelope (50c). With a score it is 150 g (70c), and with a survey 130 g (70c). So 320 members at 50c = €160, 30 soloists at 70c = €21, and 50 members at 70c = €35: €216. Sending the extra items in separate envelopes would cost 50c each instead of 20c more.

text:
Consider these statements:
1 Not all the trains were late.
2 Some of the trains were not late.
3 None of the trains were late.
4 Some of the trains were late.
Which two statements mean the same?
solution: "Not all were late" means at least one was not late, which is exactly "some were not late". "None were late" is much stronger, and "some were late" says something different again: both 2 and 4 can be true together.

text:
In a sample of double-stranded DNA, adenine and thymine together make up 46% of the bases.
What percentage of the bases are guanine?
solution: If A + T = 46%, then G + C = 54%. Guanine pairs with cytosine, so they are equal: 27% each. 23% is adenine (or thymine) alone, and 54% is G and C together.

text:
Large lakes warm up and cool down only slowly between day and night, which keeps conditions steady for the organisms in them.
Which property of water best explains this?
options: its high latent heat of vaporisation
solution: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to warm 1 kg by 1 K. Water's is very high (about 4200 J/(kg K)) because hydrogen bonds absorb energy, so a lake's temperature changes little when it gains or loses heat. Latent heat of vaporisation explains cooling by sweating instead.

text:
Four molecules of the amino acid glycine, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NO_2}\), are joined into a chain by condensation reactions.
What is the molecular formula of the product?
solution: Four glycines contain \(\mathrm{C_8H_{20}N_4O_8}\). A chain of four has three peptide bonds, and each one releases a water molecule, so subtract \(\mathrm{3H_2O}\): \(\mathrm{C_8H_{14}N_4O_5}\). Removing four waters would close the chain into a ring.

text:
Which of these features can be found in both a plant cell and a prokaryotic cell?
1 a cell wall
2 ribosomes
3 a nucleus
4 chloroplasts
solution: Both can have a cell wall (cellulose in plants, peptidoglycan in bacteria) and both have ribosomes (80S and 70S). A nucleus and chloroplasts are membrane-bound organelles found only in eukaryotes; photosynthetic bacteria have their pigments on internal membranes, not in chloroplasts. 1 and 2 only.

text: Which of these cells is likely to contain the most rough endoplasmic reticulum?
solution: Rough ER makes proteins for export. A plasma cell pours out thousands of antibody molecules a second, so it is packed with rough ER. A mature red blood cell has none at all, and fat cells, skin cells and sperm secrete little protein.

text:
Each leaf cell of a flowering plant contains 24 chromosomes. Which row is correct?

| | nucleus of a male gamete from pollen | zygote | root cell made by mitosis |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | 12 | 24 | 24 |
| row 2 | 24 | 48 | 24 |
| row 3 | 12 | 12 | 24 |
| row 4 | 6 | 24 | 12 |
| row 5 | 24 | 24 | 12 |
solution: Gametes are haploid: 12. Two gametes fuse to give a diploid zygote: 24. Mitosis keeps the number unchanged, so every body cell, root cells included, has 24. Row 1.

text:
Burning one mole of glucose releases 2800 kJ. In aerobic respiration, one mole of glucose yields about 30 moles of ATP, and each mole of ATP stores about 30.5 kJ.
Approximately how efficient is respiration at storing the energy of glucose as ATP?
solution: Energy stored in ATP = 30 x 30.5 = 915 kJ. Efficiency = 915 / 2800 x 100, about 33%. The other two-thirds is released as heat, which is part of how the body keeps warm.

text:
Three compounds of the Krebs cycle are:
1 a 4-carbon compound
2 a 6-carbon compound (citrate)
3 a 5-carbon compound
Starting with the compound that acetyl coenzyme A joins with, in what order do they appear?
solution: The 2-carbon acetyl group joins a 4-carbon compound (oxaloacetate) to form 6-carbon citrate. Citrate loses one carbon as carbon dioxide (5 carbons), then another (4 carbons), regenerating the starting compound. So 1, then 2, then 3.

text: Which list gives products of aerobic respiration in a resting muscle cell?
options: carbon dioxide, water, ATP and heat
lactic acid and carbon dioxide only
solution: Aerobic respiration oxidises glucose completely to carbon dioxide and water, capturing some energy as ATP and losing the rest as heat. Glucose and oxygen are what it uses; lactic acid is made when oxygen runs short, and ethanol only by yeast and plants.

text:
Vitamin D-resistant rickets is caused by a DOMINANT allele on the X chromosome. An affected man and an unaffected woman have children.
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1 All their daughters will be affected.
2 None of their sons will be affected.
3 Each child has a 25% chance of being affected.
solution: The man is \(X^RY\) and the woman \(X^rX^r\). Every daughter gets his \(X^R\), and one copy of a dominant allele is enough: all affected (1). Every son gets his Y and her \(X^r\): none affected (2). So each child's chance is 50%, a daughter or not, not 25% (3 wrong). 1 and 2 only.

text:
Crossover values can be read as relative distances between genes on a chromosome. Genes W, X, Y and Z lie on one chromosome, with these crossover values:
X to Z = 10
Z to W = 4
Y to X = 6
Y to W = 20
X to W = 14
Which order of the genes along the chromosome fits?
solution: Y and W are 20 apart, the largest value, so they are the two ends. X is 6 from Y and Z is 4 from W, which places X next to Y and Z next to W: Y, X, Z, W. Check the middle: X to Z = 20 - 6 - 4 = 10, and X to W = 10 + 4 = 14, both as given.

text: Two genes assort independently. Which genotype CANNOT occur among the offspring of the cross AaBb x aabb?
solution: The aabb parent can only give a and b, so every child has at least one a and one b. AaBb, Aabb, aaBb and aabb each occur with probability 1/4, but AABb would need an A from both parents.

text:
The coding strand of a section of DNA reads:
T T A G C C T T A C G A T T A G C C G G T
Read in triplets from the first base, what is the greatest number of DIFFERENT amino acids it could code for?
solution: 21 bases make 7 codons: TTA, GCC, TTA, CGA, TTA, GCC, GGT. Only 4 of them are different (TTA, GCC, CGA, GGT), and the same codon always codes for the same amino acid, so at most 4 different amino acids. It could be fewer, since different codons can code for the same amino acid.

text:
In a DNA double helix, which of the following are held to each other by hydrogen bonds?
1 bases on opposite strands
2 sugars next to each other on the same strand
3 phosphate groups on opposite strands
solution: The two strands are held together only by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (two for A-T, three for G-C) in the middle of the helix. Within a strand, sugars and phosphates are joined by covalent phosphodiester bonds, and the phosphates on the outside of the two strands are not bonded to each other.

text:
Which of the following can evolve by natural selection?
1 a population of bacteria
2 a single animal during its own lifetime
3 a population of weeds sprayed with a herbicide every year
solution: Evolution is a change in allele frequencies in a POPULATION over generations: bacteria under antibiotics and weeds under a herbicide both qualify. A single individual keeps the same genes all its life; it can adapt its behaviour or body, but it does not evolve. 1 and 3 only.

text: Which of the following would SLOW the conduction of impulses along a motor neurone?
options: a slightly higher temperature, within the normal range
the presence of a myelin sheath
saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
solution: Myelin insulates the axon so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction). Where it is damaged, as in multiple sclerosis, the impulse must travel continuously and slows down or fails. A wider axon, myelination and a little warmth all speed conduction up.

text:
Which of these happen during quiet breathing OUT?
1 The diaphragm relaxes and moves up.
2 The volume of the thorax increases.
3 The pressure in the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure.
4 The external intercostal muscles contract.
solution: Quiet exhalation is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals RELAX, the diaphragm domes upwards, the thorax gets smaller and the pressure inside rises above the air outside, pushing air out. Volume increasing and intercostals contracting belong to breathing in.

text:
Which row correctly gives the roles of the hypothalamus and of the kidneys in controlling the water content of the blood?

| | hypothalamus | kidneys |
|---|---|---|
| row 1 | releases ADH into the blood | detects the water potential of the blood |
| row 2 | detects the water potential of the blood | releases ADH into the blood |
| row 3 | detects changes in the water potential of the blood | reabsorb more or less water |
| row 4 | no role | both detect and respond |
| row 5 | reabsorbs water | produces ADH |
solution: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the change; the hypothalamus makes ADH, which the posterior pituitary releases into the blood. The kidneys are the effectors: ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed. Row 3.

text:
How does the first ionisation energy change between these neighbouring elements of period 3?

| | Na to Mg | Mg to Al | Al to Si |
|---|---|---|---|
| row 1 | increase | increase | increase |
| row 2 | decrease | decrease | increase |
| row 3 | increase | decrease | decrease |
| row 4 | increase | decrease | increase |
| row 5 | decrease | increase | decrease |
solution: Across a period the general trend is upwards, as nuclear charge rises: Na to Mg increases, Al to Si increases. The exception is Mg to Al: aluminium's outer electron is alone in a 3p orbital, higher in energy and better shielded than magnesium's 3s pair, so it is removed more easily. Row 4.

text: In a molecule of carbon dioxide, O=C=O, how many of the carbon atom's own electrons are used in bonding?
solution: Carbon has four outer electrons, and each C=O double bond uses two of them, so all four are used. The carbon is then surrounded by eight shared electrons (an octet), but four of those came from the oxygens; 6 is carbon's total electron count, including the inner two.

text: Which compound is formed when ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid in a condensation (esterification) reaction?
solution: An alcohol and a carboxylic acid join with loss of water to form an ester, named alcohol part first: ethyl ethanoate, \(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5}\), usually with an acid catalyst. Ethene comes from dehydration, bromoethane from substitution and ethanal from oxidation of ethanol.

text:
A compound consists of one benzene ring carrying a single \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2OH}\) group, and nothing else.
What is its molecular formula?
solution: Benzene is \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\); replacing one H with the side chain leaves \(\mathrm{C_6H_5}\), and \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) adds one C, three H and one O: \(\mathrm{C_7H_8O}\) (benzyl alcohol). \(\mathrm{C_6H_6O}\) is phenol, with the OH straight on the ring, and \(\mathrm{C_7H_{14}O}\) would need a saturated ring.

text:
12.0 g of magnesium is burned and 18.0 g of magnesium oxide is collected:
\(\mathrm{2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO}\)
What is the percentage yield?
[Relative atomic masses: O = 16; Mg = 24]
solution: 12.0 g of Mg is 0.50 mol, which can give at most 0.50 mol of MgO (1 : 1), and \(M_r\) of MgO = 40, so 20.0 g. Yield = 18.0/20.0 x 100 = 90%. Comparing 18.0 with 12.0 directly gives an impossible 150%.

text: Which one of these is NOT an acid-base (proton transfer) reaction?
solution: In each of the others a proton moves from an acid to a base (water even does this with itself). Zinc and hydrochloric acid is a redox reaction: zinc loses electrons (0 to +2) and hydrogen gains them (+1 to 0).

text:
How many electrons are there in total in a sulfate ion, \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)?
[Atomic numbers: O = 8; S = 16]
solution: The atoms bring 16 + 4 x 8 = 48 electrons, and the 2- charge means two extra: 50. Subtracting the charge instead of adding it gives 46.

text:
Group II of the Periodic Table contains, from top to bottom, beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium.
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1 Strontium forms the chloride \(\mathrm{SrCl_2}\).
2 Barium reacts more vigorously with water than magnesium does.
3 Calcium forms the oxide \(\mathrm{Ca_2O}\).
solution: Group II metals form 2+ ions, so their chlorides are \(\mathrm{MCl_2}\) (1) and their oxides MO, so calcium oxide is CaO, not \(\mathrm{Ca_2O}\) (3 wrong). Reactivity increases down the group, so barium reacts far more vigorously than magnesium, which barely reacts with cold water (2). 1 and 2 only.

text:
At 20 °C, 30.0 g of potassium nitrate (\(M_r\) = 101) dissolves in 100 g of water to give a saturated solution of density 1.20 g/mL.
Which calculation gives the concentration of this solution in mol/L?
solution: Moles of salt = 30.0/101. The solution weighs 100 + 30.0 = 130 g, so its volume is 130/1.20 mL, or 130/(1.20 x 1000) L. Concentration = moles / litres = \(\dfrac{30.0}{101} \times \dfrac{1000 \times 1.20}{130}\). The first option assumes the volume is just 100 mL of water.

text: Which one of these is NOT a redox reaction?
options: the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide
solution: In calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid every element keeps its oxidation number (Ca +2, C +4, O -2, H +1, Cl -1): it is an acid-carbonate reaction. Magnesium is oxidised by oxygen, chlorine oxidises iodide, peroxide oxygen (-1) goes to both -2 and 0, and electrolysis always oxidises at one electrode and reduces at the other.

subject: Physics
text: Which of these motions is closest to simple harmonic motion?
options: a ball bouncing on a hard floor
a car driving round a roundabout at constant speed, seen from above
a person walking along a pavement
a mass bobbing gently up and down on the end of a spring
a ball rolling down a slope
solution: Simple harmonic motion needs a restoring force proportional to the displacement from a centre point, which a spring provides (Hooke's law). A bouncing ball has a constant force (gravity) between impacts; motion in a circle seen from above is circular, not back and forth; walking and rolling down a slope do not oscillate about a centre.

subject: Physics
text: Which statement about heat and temperature is correct?
options: Two objects at the same temperature always contain the same amount of internal energy.
Heat flows from the object with more internal energy to the one with less, whatever their temperatures.
Heat flows from a hotter object to a colder one until their temperatures are equal.
solution: Temperature, not the total energy, decides the direction of heat flow: a cup of boiling water passes heat to a cold swimming pool even though the pool has far more internal energy. Equal temperatures can mean very different internal energies (a spoon and a lake). Temperature is in kelvin or °C, and absolute zero is -273 °C.

subject: Physics
text:
An object of mass 120 g stays exactly where it is put when fully submerged in a liquid of density 1.5 g/mL, neither rising nor sinking. It is then placed in water, of density 1.0 g/mL, and sinks to the bottom.
What force does it exert on the bottom of the container?
[Take \(g = 10\) N/kg.]
solution: Hanging still in the first liquid means its density is 1.5 g/mL, so its volume is 120/1.5 = 80 mL. In water it displaces 80 g, an upthrust of 0.8 N, against a weight of 1.2 N. The floor supplies the rest: 1.2 - 0.8 = 0.4 N.

subject: Physics
text:
A 1000 kg satellite orbits at a distance of \(7 \times 10^{6}\) m from the centre of the Earth. Use \(F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\) with \(G = 7 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}\) and the Earth's mass \(= 6 \times 10^{24}\) kg.
What is the gravitational force on the satellite, approximately?
solution: Numerator: \(7 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 10^{3} = 4.2 \times 10^{17}\). Denominator: \((7 \times 10^{6})^2 = 4.9 \times 10^{13}\). Dividing gives about \(8.6 \times 10^{3}\) N. Forgetting to square r gives \(6.0 \times 10^{10}\), not listed; slipping a power of ten in the square gives the other options.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Bag P holds 3 red balls and 1 blue ball. Bag Q holds 1 red ball and 2 blue balls. One ball is taken at random from P and put into Q. Then one ball is taken at random from Q.
What is the probability that this ball is red?
solution: If a red ball moves (probability \(\tfrac{3}{4}\)), Q has 2 red out of 4: chance \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). If a blue moves (\(\tfrac{1}{4}\)), Q has 1 red out of 4: chance \(\tfrac{1}{4}\). Total: \(\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4} \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{6}{16} + \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{7}{16}\).

subject: Mathematics
text: For every \(x > 1\), which of these expressions has the SMALLEST value?
solution: For \(x > 1\): \(x^2 > x > \sqrt{x} > 1\), and the reciprocals are below 1. Since \(x^2 > x\), its reciprocal is smaller: \(\dfrac{1}{x^2} < \dfrac{1}{x}\). Try \(x = 4\): 4, 16, 2, \(\tfrac{1}{16}\), \(\tfrac{1}{4}\).

subject: Mathematics
text: How many integers \(n\) satisfy \(|\sqrt{n} - 4| < 1\)?
solution: \(|\sqrt{n} - 4| < 1\) means \(3 < \sqrt{n} < 5\), so \(9 < n < 25\). The integers from 10 to 24 inclusive: 24 - 10 + 1 = 15. Including either endpoint (9 or 25) would wrongly give 16.
